projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Philip Marrali was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II Veteran Philip Marrali. Mr. Marrali served in the U.S. Army with the 14th Cavalry Group, 18th Recon. He served in the European Theater, and he was a prisoner of war. I'm Tom Swope and this interview was recorded at Mr. Marrali's home in [address redacted] on August 3rd, 2004. Philip was 81 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: In '41, living in -- on Barlett near Kinsman --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Kinsman Avenue.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How old were you in 1941?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Twenty years old, I went in the service.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you go to the service before the attack on Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: No, after, in 1943.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of that day, of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Yeah, we were - - we had a Filco radio, we're all sitting around the -- just so happened we were sitting around the radio, and it was about 1:00 o'clock, I think, when they -- when they announced that Pearl Harbor was attacked. Isn't that funny? It's so funny. We're all sitting around the radio that day. It was on a Sunday.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did you think when you heard that?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Well, I was kind of stunned. I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: But - -

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you working at that point? Did you have a job?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Yeah, I had a job. I -- I was working in a -- in a place we -- like a woodworking shop. That's were I worked making screens and doors, and we did weather stripping, like, put -- put metal around windows and doors and all that stuff. That's what I did.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And you thought -- when you heard that news about the attack on Pearl Harbor did you have any thought of maybe going out and signing up then?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Well, I don't know. It just - - I don't know -- it didn't -- didn't enter my mind then. I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: But my father died in 1940. I'll never forget what he said. He says, "If you have to go, go in the Army."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: And -- and he was in the First World War, but he never went over because he got the flu and he lost hearing in his - - hearing, and I guess that's why he didn't -- he didn't go overseas. He was, I think, in North Carolina, in the Army, North Carolina.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Why did you think he wanted you to go to the Army?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: I don't know. I -- when I went in, they asked - - they looked for volunteers for Navy, paratroopers, and Marines, and, he said, "How come you don't want to go in the Navy?" So I says, "I get seasick." So I went in the Army. In 1943 in February, I came home; they're celebrating my brother's birthday. When I came home they were celebrating his birthday -- my younger brother. He never -- was in the Army, but he never went overseas. He kind of missed the war.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your first day of training?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Well, it was a funny thing. I went down to Fort Riley, Kansas, with 10 jockeys. So, I figured, I'm going to be shoveling manure. They're gonna put me in the cavalry. There was a horse cavalry down there in Fort Riley. So it was at night, and I smelled the manure; I said, "Boy, this is it." So they dropped these fellows off, and they brought me somewhere else for basic training. I went - - well, just basic training. That -- after basic training, then they assign you to a different outfit, see. So after base -- three weeks of basic training, I -- I got scarlet fever, so I had to take training all over again. And after the - - after the training most of the guys they shipped 'em to Casablanca, to Africa after that, and I stayed about six months, and they shipped us to -- what was it -- Fort Lewis, Washington. I went to Fort Lewis, Washington. Then we stayed there for six months then went down to Oregon, stayed there for about six months. They went to Texas, and then from Texas we went over to Europe.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember any stories from your training? Anything unusual happen, or --

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Well, I'll tell you, Kansas City was a hellhole.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: We were coming up the drill field. It was a real funny day, like, you know, boy, you could hear a pin drop. And we're marching towards our -- our -- our barracks and the sergeant said, "Hit the dirt." And I looked up, I seen a black funnel coming straight at us. I dove in the culvert and I -- debris was flying over us, you know. Oh my god, that was - - that was unbelievable. I don't know how many fellows got killed but it just sucked up the buildings. Just left a icebox there -- like sucked up buildings. And that -- and you're marching, and it was going through water that was up to your knees. Oh, floods, oh, that place was - - I -- when I heard that song "Kansas City, Here I Come," I said, "Boy, I can't stand it." Oh, that was a -- that was terrible. Hot, oh, miserable. I couldn't wait till we got out of there. But the most beautiful place was in Washington. When the train - - we came there, seven days on that train, the train stopped, the sun was setting on a mountain near -- it looked like lava coming out, you know, there -- it was a erupting mountain. And I said, "If I ever live through this war," I said, "I want to come back here to live." I have a little mountain blood in me. And that - - oh, that place is really beautiful. So --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you assigned to an outfit at that point?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Yeah. That -- when we got there, I was assigned to the - - called the 18th Cavalry --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: -- Armor -- 18th Cavalry Armor. Then we took some training and went - - we did a lot of maneuvers in the mountains in Washington, Oregon, and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your job with the outfit?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Oh, my job was a jeep driver. I had a radio - - a radioman and a -- and a gunner in the back. He had a -- no, a .30 caliber -- .30-caliber gun in the back. And -- you want to talk about now, the war?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure, yeah. I just wondered if there's anything else from your training that you remember and then -- then you can tell me about when you went overseas.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Oh, we went - - we went -- we took the Queen Elizabeth, and they were boarding from day and night. We had -- they claimed we had 20,000 men on the ship. They were sleeping on the open decks.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: And we -- and our outfit we had a full guard duty, and my job was to make sure that when a person went out I closed this canvas and opened the other one. They had canvas doors so that submarines wouldn't, you know, see the ship.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: So that was my job. And boy, that was -- oh, my god, that was -- I don't - - I don't think we had that much room to get between our bunks, you know, packed like sardines in there. Boy, it was terrible. One morning they had a -- a boiled tomato and bacon. That was our -- our breakfast. Oh, that was terrible. Went to England. We land - - we landed in Glasgow, Scotland.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: About when did you make that crossing? Do you remember?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: About the first of September.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: The end of August, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: '44, yeah.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. The end of August, something like that. We landed -- we stayed a couple weeks in England, and we got all our equipment. Then we landed over to Cherbourg. We land in Cherbourg.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: And - - and some fellow was taking a shower, and we were bid whacking in the field there, and he got word to me that my brother was in the Cherbourg, my younger brother -- he was in the aircraft -- gun --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: So I said, "Oh, I gotta see him." So I went to the sergeant. The sergeant says, "Well, if the captain okays you can go." So I went to look for the captain, and I couldn't find him. I went back to the sergeant and says the captain okayed it. I could have got court-martialed. So, he said, "Go ahead." So I went down to the highway, bummed a ride, and it was getting late. It was around -- I don't know, it was getting dark, so I said, "Geez, boy, I gotta get back to camp." So I couldn't find his outfit, and I finally went to one U.S. sole and they told me where he was. This is really strange. I get down the highway to bum a ride to find out where he is, and there's a big truck comes by and I says, "You know where 125th ack-ack outfit is?" And the guy says, "That's my outfit." They had a big Diamond T, a real high truck. So I says, "You know Marrali?" He says, "Yeah, I know him. He's down - - he's down the highway over here. He's building a shed." So he says, "I'm gonna have some fun." He says, "When I get to him," I said, "you hide down in the cab, and I'll call him out and tell him I have another detail for him." So I hide in the cab. "Hey, Marrali, they got another detail for ya." Boy, he slammed down the tools, you know, and opens the door and sees me in there in the cab. Boy, was he tickled to see me. So we had dinner and they dispatched the jeep. I got back just in time. So I was supposed to meet him again. The next day he's waiting for me in Cherbourg and we left that night. We went -- went into Paris. We bid whacked by the Eiffel Tower.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you -- you said - - when did you make the crossing via the -- via English Channel?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: English Channel.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you - - did you stay there for just a short --

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Oh, that was around the -- around the middle of September.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you just stayed there for a very short time?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Yeah, a couple weeks.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum, yeah.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: And then we took the LST, and that was the worst experience -- I -- the worst sickness -- the worst seasickness I had in my life. I just laid over in dry heaves. See, the boat -- the amphibious is flat, you know that?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: It's flat --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The bottom half.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: -- and it -- it bobs, see. So I - - I've been in ships, and I've never been so seasick in my life. So finally at 12:00 o'clock at night the tide drops, see, about 25, 30 feet, and the whole boat is on dry land. That's why it's gotta be flat, see.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: They open the gates and -- and drive all the tanks and everything out. That's -- I don't know, those poor guys ever made that invasion. Oh, that was horrible. Oh, when I think about it -- My brother -- my older brother was -- in -- in -- in the invasion, he was a -- a welder in the Armored -- the 106th Armored --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: -- and he used to weld the tanks when -- blew up, you know. He was a welder.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: He got the Brown Star. So my younger brother met my older brother in that -- that town of -- Joan of Arc was burned at the stake.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I can't remember, but I know what you're talking about.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Yeah, that's where they met, see. I met my younger brother; my younger brother met my older brother.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's great.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: And he met my neighbor too. My older brother met my neighbor in -- in some town in France.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were on your way to Paris then; right?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Yeah, we bid whacked one -- one night in the Eiffel Tower -- you know that park?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Had our tents there. Next morning half of the outfit was gone. They forgot to come back. So they had us -- they had to lead an advance party to round 'em up. Then we went into Luxembourg and Bastogne. We bid whacked one night in Bastogne, and then we went into a -- a town. We had to occupy this town of Kopashite(ph) -- Kopashite(ph), Germany. And we were there for about -- let's see, October, November, and -- and the 16th is when the Battle of the Bulge broke. We were out on the Siegfried line -- holding the Siegfried line. And --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your first day in combat when you were under fire?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Well, that was a -- let's see, September -- it was around October -- sometime the beginning of October. That's when -- we were just holding the town and they were shelling and bombs coming over and -- But the German people they're -- most of them are Catholic. They're wonderful people.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So in that town they were fairly friendly to the ___?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: I don't know if I should tell you this story, but -- I don't know if you could put it in or not. Well, I killed a cow for the old lady. There was two old ladies there with a couple of kids, and they invited me to have supper with them. So I'm looking out the window -- the windows open like -- like French windows, you know, like, you know -- I think that saved my life. A shell came over the top and landed in a pile of manure, and the next thing I knew, I'm laying on the floor with a face full of horse manure, you know. They were in the -- I was like in the family room, like, you know. And they come in running and they saw that it was okay, they laughed, you know. I -- and then I was going in the kitchen to wash my face, and I looked over, I see the head of the cow in there and I said, "Well." I took off.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You didn't stay for dinner?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: And that was the funniest thing that happened, you know. That's why they -- they always tease me. That's why I'm so dark. I -- I got a face full of horse manure.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: But that -- that was -- I was a foot away from the window and blew every window from that side of the house out, and I didn't get a scratch -- unbelievable. Now that -- that -- I think that was a miracle. 'Cause -- that -- I had a lot of close calls. Believe me I had my guardian angel telling me things. I hesitated doing certain things that saved my life.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were those French windows opened?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Yeah. See, the concussion blew them open, and the glass flew this way, see.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: And that's why I said that -- that maybe the windows weren't locked or something --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Exactly.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: -- they're French windows, see.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Instead of blowing them back at ya.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Yeah, and the manure came and it -- it landed in maybe about a six-foot pile of manure. The motor shell came over the top of the house, see.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: And went down in the manure, buried itself, and it -- a shell -- a motor shell is about that big. You know what a motor shell is?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: I was only a foot away from the window. I didn't get a scratch. I was --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Would you have gotten in trouble for fraternizing with them?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: No, no. They -- they're -- oh, we stayed by their houses. You could stay in their -- they wanted you to stay in their houses.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, okay, yeah.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Yeah. Well that's what saved my life, see. When -- when the Battle of the Bulge broke through, I ran in the house and what -- the walls were thick like that, the shells would just bounce off them houses. The shells -- the stone walls -- and my buddy -- the one I showed you a picture of -- we were in a machine gun, we had a .30-caliber machine gun, and we're fighting over it. So I says, "All right, so, okay you take the machine gun; I'll cover the side window." And I fired a Thompson submachine gun for eight hours without -- that's what happened my last -- that's when the Germans surrendered. I had three -- three rounds left in the gun. So, anyway, after the Germans surrendered, 4:30 at night I came down, this fellow was laying there on the floor all blood coming out of him, you know. He was one of my -- matter of fact, I gotta answer one of his letters. He lives in California. So, I said, "Well he's gone." So they finally round up the guys, they got on the jeep -- one fellow what saved his -- he was telling me the story -- one saved their life is this one fellow spoke German, see. And that's what saved them -- see they were killing all the prisoners, like the few prisoners.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: They captured, they were killing 'em. So I went Cherbourg -- the day before I got the boat I was in Camp Lucky Strike and looking at this fella, I says, "Boy, he looks familiar." That was him.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So he made it back?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: I said, "Geez, I never" -- it was Bob -- I said, "Geez, I -- I never thought I'd see you alive." And he was really shot up. And he says, they treated so good. He said the Ger -- the German, the nurses were sneaking him beer. They really -- of course, he was a good looking guy, black, wavy hair. Boy, women were crazy about him. He had more women in the -- in the Army and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you in that same village, then, when the Battle of the Bulge started, the one you talked about earlier?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Yeah --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: On the Siegfried line?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Kopashite(ph) -- Kopashite(ph), yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what else do you remember about the first day of the Battle of the Bulge?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Well, the first day at 4:30 Germans surrendered, and they -- they were coming in. The first thing they wanted -- cigarettes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Cigarettes. So they -- they got all their guns and threw them in -- all our guns -- threw them in the -- in the middle of the street with gasoline and burned 'em.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Threw gasoline and burned 'em, and then a few minutes later they told us got orders to destroy everything and fall back.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: So I -- I -- I had a pack of -- I -- I took whatever I could find to put on my back, and I had two guns and I had another -- I took -- I found another gun so I took two guns and then we took off into the woods -- had to get a word to our lieutenant -- I got a picture of the lieutenant there. Anyway, he must have got word of it that the Germans were taking our vehicles and wearing our uniforms, see, at that time. So, a convoy went by, and we were hiding in the woods and -- so they wouldn't see us. After the convoy went by and we got up looked for -- for our lieutenant and he was gone. You know, it was so dark you couldn't see a hand in front of ya. He was gone. So I wound up with nine fellas, and I don't know -- we were -- we were all confused, man, that those damned big vines -- what the hell they call those things? Some kind of funny thing that looks like a long -- a fern -- fern, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Big -- about six feet high there in the woods.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: And we finally got out of that, and we were walking along the -- the road -- there was a hard-surfaced road -- and the German says, "Halt." And, boy, I'll tell you my knees were knocking. I said -- we almost hugged each other, and they opened up with burp guns -- burp, burp, burp -- they're like German -- they call it a burp gun. And we didn't see them. They had white uniforms on, see, that's why we didn't see 'em. And we didn't have none. So, I told the guys, I said, "Get off on the road." See, the road was -- there was no snow on the road and we were in the -- that's why they saw us. So we got off the road -- got up to the road and they stopped shooting. I says, "Man, we better" -- then all of a sudden they -- they started the tanks. They had tanks, see --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: -- and there was a patrol with tanks. So, I said, "Man, we better get outta here." So we went -- it was like a farm and then like a woods in the background, so we got -- we were out on -- on the -- it was like a farmland. They saw us again they started shooting at us again. They saw us taking off in the field. So we got into the woods and I -- then I started hearing these guns going off, you know. I distinguished the sound was like 105, I think. Man, it was big, big flashes and I says, "Boy, those -- that's the Americans -- the American -- that's the American guns." So we kept following sound, and then I -- we -- we heard American voices like, you know, they said, "Hitch 'em up." I told -- oh, those are Americans over there. So I told the guys to stay in the woods. I'm gonna go and see if I get contact with those guys. I went over barbed-wire fences -- most barbed-wire fence -- oh, that -- they're all mined with mines and grenades.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: So one fella says -- I yelled -- you know, I says, "Hold your fire," I says, "we're lost American patrol coming in." And then the guy says, "Come forward me recognize who go there." The guy's holding a machine gun. They had .30 calibers. They had one guy holding the belt, you know, the bullets. He says, "Man, you're lucky. We was ready to open up on you. We saw you out there." They was shooting anything that moved. So I call -- I went and got the rest of the guys, and I -- I said, "You better get out outta" -- I says, "the tanks are -- are right behind us, coming out." He said, "I can't -- we know it. We know it." So it was 106th ack-ack. They was firing up those big bullets shooting at airplanes that was their outfit. So we got on the trucks, and they start falling back, and sure enough, we -- we had a service company they had all the supplies there, like, you know, supplies -- and they had us all surrounded and shooting at us for a couple days. We couldn't do nothing. So they made a truce then they -- they surrendered, and that's -- that was the 21st -- the 21st of December. That's when I was captured. The only reason they captured -- there was -- I don't know 3-, 400, something like that. I think it was -- that's the only reason they kill -- but they were killing a lot of fellows.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. So that's why -- it was such a large group. You think that's why they didn't execute them?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Did -- you -- on what was it on Nam -- was it --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Malmedy?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Malmedy, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: I was there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were in Malmedy?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: No. I wasn't there during the war.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: I was there after. I was there --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was it later?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Yeah. I was on a -- a -- a 30th anniversary of the Battle of the Bulge.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, yeah?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Yeah. That's where I met Westmoreland.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum, okay.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Yeah. So, you want to talk about that then, huh?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were captured on the 21st?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: The 21st, yeah. And then we marched to -- what's the name of that -- marched to Stalin Fort B, that's where they put us, we marched, Stal -- that was New Year's night when we got there. But Christmas Eve, that's the first day it cleared up, and we were standing there -- they -- I don't know what -- I think because they locked us in these boxcars -- it was on the side track, there was no train or anything, it blocked us in. The B-2s were going off, see, and I heard a -- a thunder. The sky cleared up and I -- I turned around, I seen -- that's the first time I seen the B-2 go off, you know. And just -- it was a white vapor going through the sky. And I said, "That's probably why they locked us in here. Maybe they're afraid somebody's going to escape and reveal where they're launching the B-2s," see.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: So about 1:00 o'clock the bombers came over, and -- and I happened to get captured with four of my buddies. Isn't that strange? Four of my -- we're all scattered all over.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: It was four of my buddies all sitting against the wall in a boxcar, and I was lying against his knees, and he was the last fella. So, they -- the bombers came -- the fighters came down scraped the boxcars. And I was going to take his place -- he went and did his business in a helmet -- there was an opening on the end. So I said, "Well," -- something told me I'll wait till he comes back, you know. I won't take his spot because my back was hurting against his knees, you know, packed in those boxcars. Sure enough, they wounded my three buddies and killed him. He was killed. And I looked up; the whole top was almost sheared off the top of the boxcar.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: So, they -- they took off -- the Germans and left us, see. They went up to Salton field, so I know somebody -- I guess the boxcars were all shot up, and somebody managed to get up, and they're opening all the boxcars. I guess they knew -- they finally realized that there was Americans locked in there, so they just scraped over one time, see. And they took off, and in the meantime, there was anti-aircraft guns near us. We made it up to this open field and we made U.S. POW over there. So the fires came down treetop level. Boy, they knocked all those damn anti-aircraft guns out, but the mean -- before they did that they hit a -- a B-17. It was so funny that it cut in half, and I saw the -- the tail-end gunner bail out -- tail-end gunner?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: And we -- after it was all over with there were all the dead guys. They put them on -- on the platform and the live guys they put 'em in the -- the guys that were wounded they put them in the -- in that railroad station. And we can't figure out why this guy, he -- he bailed out and didn't have a mark on his body, this one -- this one -- the tail-end gunner of this B-17.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: So, then that happened during the -- oh, yeah, before that, six hours after I was captured, I saw Rundstedt, General Rundstedt.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: And there was on a big touring car and they had a -- they were taking movies of us.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Yeah, the tripod -- and he's standing like this, you know, with his big leather coat, and I says, "Son of a gun." Then found out that he, you know, that he was Rundstedt, in charge of the Battle of the Bulge.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did he say anything to the prisoners?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: No, no. We were, oh, I don't know, maybe from here to the end of the street.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: And we was marching and they were standing on the big touring car.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: You know, the -- it was all --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right, right.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: -- like a convertible.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Exactly.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: And they had a tripod on there, and he's standing next to the guy taking movies of us.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you might be in a propaganda film somewhere from the Germans, huh?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I suppose it's possible in their archives.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: So -- let's see what else that happened? Went from there -- oh, yeah, we marched -- we marched to little towns and they thought that -- they thought that -- I guess I was in the armor we had those helmets like -- like the Air Force, you know. Almost like a Air Force uniform and they would spit at ya and call you a (luke wopper swine houser (ph)), you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Really, the citizens, the people?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Yeah. So they took all my damn clothes away from me -- all those they -- and -- let's see, what -- I had some cold clothes, like a green cap and a brown uniform -- I don't -- coat -- I don't know what they -- they got these -- I don't know they're Russian or what. Matter of fact, when I was in a -- working over there, the German -- a girl called me a -- a Russki, thought I was Russian. That stuff -- the uniform I had must have been Russian.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So did they take away your American uniforms?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you think they were using them for the infiltrating?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: I don't know, I don't know. So we were in Stalin Fort B with the British, and we got there Chris -- New Year's -- New Year's Eve we got the first hot meal we had. We had something like oatmeal -- they gave us in a can. They gave us a shot in our chest, I don't know what's this for. And I was there with the -- with the British, and we had tea eight times a day. They gets five -- five potatoes like golf balls -- lived on that. That's all we had. And then they -- I worked in Halle, Germany on the railroad -- they put us to work on the railroads -- worked on railroads in Halle, Germany. And we -- they put us in the cellar, it was a beer joint, I don't know -- it was the back or upstairs -- it was a big house -- put us in the cellar. We had straw, and, man, it was rats like that, sewer rats down there. They had no heat, and worked -- like, we get up 3:00 or 4:00 o'clock in the morning, and take streetcars, and work wherever the tracks were blown up, and went to work on the -- on the railroad. And --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What city was that near?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: It was in Halle, Germany.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Halle, right, okay.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: So when we first got there, they give you a bowl of turnips soup, and these Ru -- there was -- maybe about 20 -- the Russians. They -- they must have come from someplace else and we took their place. Every one of them got up and give us their meal, and I never forget that. This Russian he didn't give me the spoon. I got the spoon downstairs, he has a little swastika on him, must have been the Air Force.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: And every time they stole something they always -- if the guards weren't looking, they'd share it. But we weren't supposed to talk to anybody except the fellows we worked with, see, over there. And let's see -- oh, one time they blew the boxcars up, and he managed to sneak a little cup of caviar -- cup of caviar. And I said, "Here I am a prisoner of war eating caviar."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: And then one time the little German girl was running with a big hunk of cheese, and the German guy chased her. They go up the boxcars; she stole the cheese or something.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: And you're chasing after her to get the cheese away but -- yeah, the Russians were crazy. One time this -- a guy was going by -- they had -- they buried their potatoes in the mound, like, you know, and then when they need them they go there and get them. And so there's a little horse and a cart, and the fellow's going past us, you know, to work on the railroads -- a road there, and he goes -- he lifts the sack of potatoes off the cart. The Russians, boy they were crazy. They didn't -- when they were hungry, boy, they did -- they did anything. He grabbed the potatoes and right behind there's, like a toolshed over there, like -- or something like where we got our tools. That's -- that was the funny -- the funny thing that happened. We -- we -- you put the ties in the railroad. See, the tracks were all blown up and then they have -- they put a one track here and they -- they bring all the supplies in, rails and all that stuff, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: The rail -- so once we get all the ties in they were like crooked. See, we had to hit the ties and straighten them. So we're -- we're three or four fellows there and we -- we'd hit them with something, I don't know -- hit the ties to straighten it out, like -- so we couldn't get together so I got a brainstorm going, "Yo ho, Yorkneck." The Russians were -- the Russians heard, they're laughing, you know. Then we hit the tie, like, you know. Boy, those Russians -- we had more fun over there -- they're crazy. So, the 13th of -- the 13th of April -- no, the 13th? I think it was the 13th. I can't remember the days too good. They -- they bombed this place right near us, five kilometers from where we were was a big railroad yard, and -- and we were coming home on the electric train. See, what -- what passenger -- like a passenger train -- we're coming on that, and it was -- the light was red so the guard took off. I guess he had to go to the bathroom, and in the meantime the light changed and the train took off. So we had to walk and we had to walk across the railroad yard. Oh, it was huge, like from here maybe to the corner. Big railroad yard and then we're walking across, they stopped, they dropped parachutes with flares, lit everything like daytime, and we had -- by the time we got to our building the burp alarms ringing, you know, they go {indicating}. That means they're coming. They go {indicating}. That means that they're overhead.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: So, by that time they're overhead and we got -- we had trenches in back -- backyard and they were going for 48 hours, day and night, the late-action blockbusters. So we went there to work with the 13th, and I told the guys -- I'll never forget this -- I'm standing there looking -- holes -- I'm telling you won't believe they're -- Russians -- they killed a lot of Russians. There was -- they were near there. You could put this whole house in there -- the huge holes. The concussion was so bad it was like somebody smashing my ears five kilometers away -- blowed all the windows out in our -- in the building we were.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And, I said, "This -- this job's going to take 50 years." All those crater holes. So two minutes later, the guard says Roosevelt died. So I -- we didn't -- we didn't believe it, you know -- so -- thought it'd be propaganda. So, a few minutes later, we're still standing there, we never started to work yet, all of a sudden I heard firing in the distance, you know. I said, "Wow, they're -- they're, they're close," you know, the Americans. I know all this firing, I know that the Americans were close so they -- well -- then we start marching for another 10, 11 days. We marched up to the Baltic Sea in the -- in the border of Poland.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Right at the edge of the border of Poland. So, let's see --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was that march like?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Oh, the -- until you get -- you get so hungry -- you don't feel hungry. You just feel like you was on a desert, you break for water, but lucky that we, you know, when we stopped, we ate snow, see. One time we stopped, I managed to dig up a turnip. I don't know if it was a sugar turnip or something, and I put it in my pocket, and I had one piece of black bread with molasses on it -- they give us that on Christmas Eve -- and that one turnip for 17 days. We marched all -- we marched -- it was about 11 days, I think, 11 days after I was captured till we got to prison. It was New Year's Day we got to the prison camp, and, let's see, we -- marched -- we marched to Poland and that's -- oh, yeah, then we got to the -- the Russians. Then we heard the Russian guns --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: -- you know, the cannons in the distance. And one Russian flew over us tipped its wings, you know, we saw the star. He identified us. So we carried a white flag with a stick -- he identified us that -- that was American. And, boy, this one guard -- I'm telling ya, I never seen a person -- he turned white as a sheet. This guard, he was so scared he turned white as a sheet. And we start marching back, we start -- we start getting away from there, see. Then we marched -- I don't know four or five hours -- something like that and some little -- there was some little Wiz -- Wiz -- Wizdin(ph) or something like that, I can't remember the name of the town. So then they -- we're coming to that town and they met one couple Americans and they surrendered. They -- they gave up their guns and everything to these guys, and we marched over to this -- this little town. Everybody was -- had white flags hanging out and we were by a -- a field and, of course, you know, it took time before they got supplies up and get us some food -- but hundreds of thousands -- as far as I could see, there was all kinds of prisoners coming in there. So these Arabians, they had turbans on --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Then they had a pig on sticks, see. So I met a -- a American guy give me a pack of cigarettes. So I went hungry, you know, I didn't eat for eight days. So I -- I told him -- I says, "I'll give you the pack of cigarettes; you give me something to eat. You know, some of that pig." I guess they didn't kill it yet. I got some of the pig, and I don't know I built a fire or something over there -- in the field over there. Boy, I got sick. I'll never forget that. I got friends -- of course, you know, I didn't have any food for, you know, four months. So I got sick on that. Then, finally, I don't know -- it was how many days later, they finally come with trucks to get us out of there. And all the women wanted to jump on our trucks, you know, they were afraid, you know, the Russians were gonna come there, and, you know -- you know what they did to them, the women especially -- you know, the Russians.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: So they finally got us to -- they brought us back to the same place where I was working Halle, Germany. It was the Air Force Academy there, that's where I picked up a lot of junk -- the Air Force Academy there. And -- what was it, I think the eighth or something like that, the -- they Germans surrendered. As a matter of fact, the -- they had an American guy chasing the German airplane flew over me, and I was sitting on the balcony, I'll never forget that. It was a -- like a -- I was sitting by a stone wall that bullet came right over my head, hit the wall. They were celebrating all drunk, smashing cars.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Oh, there -- it will was holy hell. And I was just sitting there watching, you know. They had cars and they'd jump out of 'em and smash 'em. As a matter of fact, we had a truck we were trying to get that started, we had a furnace on it -- trying to get that started -- have some fun with it. So, anyway, they flew us out from there to the Reims, then went to Reims and Le Havre -- Reims. Yeah, from there we flew to Reims -- Reims, France. From Reims we flew to Le Havre. They flew us out with airplanes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: And then, I can't remember where we took the boat. You know, it's funny, I'll tell you a funny story. This is very strange. I had -- I had dreams that I was always home in my khakis walking around, and I told the fellas, I said, "If we live -- the war's going to be over and we're going to be home in the summertime." And sure enough -- and I -- I would -- I had a dream that I was walking around the back of the boat. The boat wasn't pulling forward -- backwards, you know, in the pier -- and sure enough, I'm walking the boat and the boat's back in the pier and I'm looking, and I said, "Geez, I had all these dreams three months ago."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: And sure enough we're home in our khakis in the summer. Isn't that funny? I had -- that was a dream. That's strange, wasn't it?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, you say you picked up a lot of souvenir things before you left Halle and went back to Camp Lucky Strike; right?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, what kind of stuff did you pick up ___+?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Oh, I got -- I got stuff down in the basement. I don't know. I got them in a big glass case.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You got -- you showed me some photos here, photos of Hesse? Is that a photo of Hesse in there?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Yeah, that's --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And you have the negatives, too.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You got those there?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: That's Hitler standing by the car.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: That's -- that's one in the back there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: That -- Hesse --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, you're right.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: That's Hesse.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's very interesting.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: I -- I see if I could find -- I think I got a photostatic copy back here.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How long were you in Camp Lucky Strike then before you boarded that ship?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Camp Lucky Strike? I don't know, maybe a week or a few days -- Lucky Strike.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Then we got home -- I got home around -- around the end of June, I think. Somewhere around the end of June I got home. Oh -- oh another thing, see -- see, I can't remember all it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's okay.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: We were -- we were still -- I could still see land because when I saw -- I didn't bother looking when we -- we ran into a mine -- a floating mine. So the boat circled around and when the boat turned around and I could just see the outskirts of land. We're pretty far out. Then they -- they were -- they blew it up. They'd start firing at it -- and they blew it up. It must have been the mine, the anchor, you know, so far underneath the waterline.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: And it must have broke loose and floated up. And going there, a day out of England we almost got torpedoed. Shot four torpedoes at us and the guy was on Channel 25, the German captain, he fired -- they interviewed him and they fired four torpedoes at us and the last torpedo, he almost got us. They jerked the ship, just missed us -- and boy, everybody was thrown all over the ship.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Then there was -- there was 20,000 men. Boy, if they would have hit that ship, boy, it would have been a disaster. And then it was B -- BBYs or something coming on.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: PBY; right?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Yeah, they were coming out looking for 'em. They -- I guess they knew it. I guess they knew it -- of course, they got things -- I could tell the submarines, you know. We went unescorted too, all the way across. We were going like that, zigzagging all the way across. Yeah, I can remember that. Yeah, I had a lot of --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reunion with your family like when you got back?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Oh, my grandmother was still living. She was dancing with my brother. She was about I don't know 75, 80, or something like that. They were so happy. All us brothers managed to come home. But I lost two of them, both died of heart attacks. One was only 40 years old; the one was in -- the welder. And then my other with ack-ack, he died at 52. Both had heart attacks. Yeah, that was -- just like that. One day you're with 'em, the next day they're gone, yup. So, well when I met -- I met Westmoreland, I was 50 feet from Patton's grave. When I turned around, Westmoreland was behind me, and oh, I said, "What should I do?" So, we shook hands and walked to Patton's grave, you know -- Luxembourg. So, here I says, "I'm going to see a dead general; there's a live one behind me." And Hodges, he came up to our position, unescorted. He had .50 caliber on the jeep, and when he -- when he turned -- we were guarding the road like that -- we had a -- and there were two roads coming into town so we went this way, and this is Germany this way, so he -- he went this way, and as soon as he -- he opened up his .50 caliber -- just firing that .50 caliber. He just -- him and the jeep driver came up there. And Hodges -- that's right, I saw Hodges. And I saw -- what was it, Bradley.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, yeah?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: I was in Fort Lewis -- I was buying something I turned around we almost hugged each other -- Bradley. I saw his museum, and I saw his grave in Arlington.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But when you saw Westmoreland that -- you said that was 30 years later?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Yeah 30th anniversary of the Battle of the Bulge, yeah. I saw Patton's grave. And I'll -- I'll tell ya, I says, "You know who I really think who is a real general? Patton." He was blood and guts, so they call him. He was a real general.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did guys like him, you think?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: He was -- I think they did. He -- he was a rough guy, but he was -- he was real -- a real soldier. I think he was a real soldier. And the Battle of the Bulge, you know, we knew then. We knew that in -- around the beginning of October. We captured Germans, and at night you can hear -- you can hear them -- the tanks and everything. I even got proof over here. This guy he went on patrol and he heard all the tanks and everything. Was it the last -- the last patrol out of Kopashite(ph). This -- this fellow is a wonderful person. His father got the last patrol.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: This is all. His -- his father's the one that got the reunion started. He went to Washington, all the people were lost and he got our first reunion started in Fort Riley, Kansas.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So is that the guy in your outfit that wrote this?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. That -- this is the guy in my outfit here. It's the story about the last patrol out of Kopashite(ph).

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where does he live?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: He's in Oregon.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: In Oregon. There's a lot of -- I don't know. I got a lot of stuff in bags. This -- this is just some books. I got enough books to start a library. I got -- you know the -- what's his name -- MacDonald -- wrote the story of the Battle of the Bulge -- MacDonald.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: MacDonald?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Yeah. I got -- I saw him and he was on the reunion.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Yeah, I got the book too. He wrote the first story of the Battle of the Bulge. He was on the reunion. Here's -- here's another one. This is something about the Battle of the Bulge -- one fellow -- this is the fellow who wrote to me. This -- this -- this is -- let's see, A Time for Trumpets. Yeah -- Battle of the Bulge -- MacDonald.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: I met him. He thought I didn't have this, but I have his book. Oh, I met a lot of famous people. This one fellow was my outfit he was Indian, he played in Gunsmoke.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: And he had a -- he had a ranch in San Fernando Valley. So he wanted to bring me. He kind of liked me, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: He wanted me to -- maybe because I was dark I might have been Indian or something. A lot -- they take me for Indian. So he wanted to take me down to his ranch. He used to -- he used to be the stunt -- you know, he looked like the guy to fall off a horse.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Stuntman. Right, right, right. {Break in tape}

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Yeah. So they had '34 Chevy, pile of junk. I said, "Oh, you guys never gonna make it." We're in Oregon about 500 miles from the -- so I said, "You guys never gonna make it down there." So, sure enough I didn't go with them, they came back three or four days late, they snapped an axle or something, and I'm pulling guard duty we had to guard -- {Break in tape}

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: All right. Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: So anyways, digging this hole, and I says, "You see why I don't want to go with you guys." Says, "Oh, you lousy ___+." He started chasing him with the shovel, you know. And matter of fact, I got some literature, although I don't know, he had some writings in the paper. I don't know where I have it. I guess I have it in all my stuff there. But -- Sergeant Vaughn he was a hell of a nice guy. Boy, you couldn't find -- he had the silver -- silver pistols and they -- he wanted to take 'em to Europe.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, great.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: And they -- they wouldn't let him -- they wouldn't let him take 'em.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: They wouldn't let him bring the guns. And he played in Gunsmoke, a lot of parts in Gunsmoke. He was -- and I never knew it, he was part Indian.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: He was Indian. I never knew that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any other vivid memories come to mind about your experiences during World War II?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Let's see. Who'd I meet? Boy, I met a lot of my buddies. He was wounded. Well, I was going over to Europe. I got a letter he was -- we were -- we were buddies from -- my god, since '39.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: I'm walking down the street one ___+ behind me -- he got wounded in France -- probably had to take his leg off -- shell ricocheted off his leg. He was my neighbor down the street from where I lived.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have some close buddies during -- before you were captured?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Oh, yeah. There was three of us. This one fellow he went -- I was telling ya, he went -- I don't know -- he was out there with the motor shell and he was knocking the Germans off it. I guess he got the Silver Star. And he's down in Fairmont, West Virginia. So he had --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: [Interrupts]

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: -- he had --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: [Interrupts]

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: What, go ahead?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I was just going to ask you about life in the POW camp, if you had any other --

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Well it was kind of rough. We had -- one time they had -- these shoes are wedged, see -- had no rubber shoes or anything, and I found a pair of wooden shoes and I put them on and the snow was thick on the bottom and my foot would spin around. You know, that was terrible to be -- to be cold and hungry, man, we had to sleep with no heat. And we had a potbelly stove but you couldn't find anything. You couldn't find anything. You couldn't find a piece -- a piece of wood. Piece of twig you couldn't find. And then people were out to snatch all that up, you know, for heat. Couldn't find a piece of wood, they had no heat. And fleas, boy, oh, the fleas. They never bit me though. A lot of guys had the trouble with fleas. And they had a lot of ties over here that never got back -- all the tracks been blown up and you never got back to the -- to your -- to the building where we lived, and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get any parcels, or mail, while you were in the camp?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Oh, yeah. It was nine weeks after we got a Red Cross parcel. We split it up so many fellas -- that, that thing saved your life because you -- what the hell you call it -- it was lack in vitamins. A lot of times you, you would -- everything would get like blurred, you know. And big sores with puss, your legs, and -- well that -- that thing saved us till we got those vitamin pills. That saved -- after nine weeks till we finally got a -- a Red Cross parcel. Just living on a bowl of turnips, you know, and -- and whatever we could -- couldn't find too much steel. But the guys, some guys they the luck, they worked on farms, you know. They had -- they had something to eat more than us. But we didn't have much. And --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get the chance to do anything for R and R, in the camp any -- any breaks any way to pass the time or amuse yourselves or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Oh, on Sunday we had one fella -- we used to sing. It was like a gospel singer or someone we had, yeah. He was like, supposed to be like the minister. And one fellow he was -- I remember he traded his food out for cigarettes. He was like a walking skeleton. We finally -- there was a raid and he finally disappeared and we never saw -- never knew what happened to him -- finally disappeared. Yeah, but, you know, you work out on the railroads they used to have a train and everybody would get on the train to take you away -- it was a raid, but the bombs are coming down so fast you didn't have time to get on that train. We'd just take off for open fields. They were coming down like rain on ya.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How -- how did the guards treat you, for the most part?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Well, one -- one guard -- one guard tried -- he beat me up and we were waiting on the platform for this train to come home and a bunch of dive bomb -- fighter -- fighter planes came over, and they're diving straight at us, see. We thought they were gonna -- they were gonna go after us, but they -- they turned over and they went over someplace else and shot up. So in the meantime, we all -- we all scattered, you know, ran away, and then we came back. This one guard starts slashing me in the face from behind, you know, and I went after him, and he got the bayonet, and the guy grabbed me. He was ready to jab me with the bayonet. That -- that -- I was looking for him. I was so mad. But they -- every so many months, they changed guards, see.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Every week or two weeks they changed the guards. We had one guy from Russia, he lost an eye. He was a miserable son of a gun. He was a miserable guy. And we had this Polish fella, he was about 25, 30 years old, and he was -- he spoke English, see. So he was a boss, like, and he was a hell of a nice guy -- Polish kid. So meantime there was a raid and we were both running away to the railroad yards, and I'm running with him, you know, and there was a rabbit in front of him. He catches the rabbit and hits it behind his head, you know, killed it, and he hides it in his jacket. And the funny thing he says, he says, "Come over -- come over my house tonight for supper." It was a joke you know. I don't know. He was like a trustee or something I don't know where he lived.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: But --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But they had him serving as a guard, huh?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Yeah -- no. He was a boss like, see, we couldn't --couldn't understand the Germans telling you what to do -- they get the shovel, you couldn't understand.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. So he was brought in to kind of ___?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: So I had my wristwatch. They never took it away from me, you know. I had a loose dial on there. So I -- I asked him, I said, "Geez, I come here today," I said, "what -- what can I get for my wristwatch?" You know, they never took my wristwatch, but it's funny, I don't know why. So, he said, "I'll get you a loaf of bread." So he got me a loaf of bread that day, and I had this big coat with a rope or wire or something around it, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: And I -- I hid the bread in there, and I don't know how I cut it, it was hard as a rock. I guess they say that bread can last ten years ___+.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, yeah?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Yeah. I don't know, it's like a pumpernickel bread. So I got a loaf of bread for my wristwatch. So, I don't remember any other things.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Think that covers it?

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Think that's about it. Well, I got a lot of stuff -- after the war.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: I met a lot of people. Oh, let's see. What else -- Marshal. What else -- what other general did I meet? There's -- there's another story.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Pretty interesting book.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: See -- see, we were holding these towns -- all these towns here.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: And this is Saint Vith, and here's the town of Kopashite(ph), see?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: And we used to contact the people from towns -- they contacted the different towns, bringing mail or something like that, and we got shot up a couple times over there, you know, they didn't -- they didn't -- they missed me. The one time was so damn close it made my ears ring. We had -- when you slowed down to go around a corner, see, they'd hide in these like in the forest, all pine trees. They take hot shots at you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, great.

sp.speaker: Philip Marrali
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.
